title: EADV: Autonomous AI Can Increase Clinical Capacity for Dermatologists
source_used: Bioengineer.org (relaying Scienmag); HealthDay page returned no text
key_facts: An autonomous AI system in two UK hospitals followed 8,391 patients on urgent suspected skin cancer pathways, presented at the EADV Congress 2026 in Vienna.
The system, a CE-marked Class III medical device, discharged benign lesions on its own and routed higher-risk cases to teledermatologists.
86% of offered patients consented; the pathway covered 94% of urgent suspected skin cancer referrals at the two sites.
The AI discharged 31% of patients at one hospital and 25% at the other without specialist review.
Researchers estimate 2,851 clinician hours saved, about 62% more capacity, or over 8,500 extra face-to-face appointments in 16 months.
Sensitivity exceeded 98% for invasive melanoma, squamous cell and basal cell carcinoma, with specificity of 72.1%.
Surveillance found six false negatives (five basal cell carcinomas, one melanoma in situ); no adverse outcomes were identified in available follow-up.
Lead author Dr Lucy Thomas of Chelsea & Westminster Hospital NHS Foundation Trust calls it proof of concept; La Roche-Posay partly supported the work.
quote_evidence: We believe the greatest value of autonomous AI lies not in the technology itself, but in the specialist capacity it unlocks.
If these findings are replicated across larger populations and different healthcare settings, autonomous AI could become an important part of creating a more sustainable dermatology service.
why_it_matters_hint: Autonomous AI cleared about half of urgent skin referrals without a face-to-face visit, freeing specialist time, but six missed cancers were found after discharge.
event_date: Presented at EADV Congress 2026, reported 5 Oct 2026
notes: HealthDay page returned HTTP 200 with no text. Read Bioengineer.org, which credits Scienmag. Conference results, not peer-reviewed publication as far as the text says.
